questions.keyword: Business structures — sole proprietorship, general/limited partnership, LLC, C corporation, S corporation: formation, liability protection, continuity, taxation, management; rights and duties of owners
questions.text: A corporation's shareholders personally guarantee a lease, loan, and equipment contract for the corporation. The corporation subsequently fails to pay these obligations. A plaintiff argues the 'corporate veil' should be pierced, making shareholders personally liable for all corporate debts (not just the guaranteed obligations). Under what circumstances will courts pierce the corporate veil?

answers.text: Courts pierce the corporate veil whenever a corporation fails to pay its debts — limited liability is automatically eliminated upon insolvency
Courts never pierce the corporate veil — personal guarantees are the only mechanism by which shareholders can become personally liable

Courts pierce the corporate veil when: the corporation is used as a mere instrumentality (alter ego) of the shareholders; corporate formalities are disregarded (no board meetings, comingled funds, no separate books); or the corporate form is used to commit fraud or injustice against creditors
Courts pierce the corporate veil only when shareholders have majority voting control and use that control to cause the corporation to breach contracts

explanations.a: Corporate insolvency alone does not pierce the veil — the purpose of limited liability is precisely to protect shareholders when the business fails. Creditors take the risk of corporate insolvency by extending credit to the entity rather than requiring personal guarantees.
explanations.b: Courts DO pierce the corporate veil in appropriate circumstances — it is neither impossible nor limited to guaranteed debts. Veil-piercing is an equitable doctrine that is available in specific circumstances.
explanations.c: Piercing the corporate veil (alter ego doctrine): courts may disregard the corporate entity and hold shareholders personally liable for corporate obligations when: (1) Alter ego/mere instrumentality: the corporation is not treated as a separate entity — the shareholder uses the corporation as their personal tool (e.g., pays personal bills with corporate funds, treats corporate assets as their own); (2) Failure to observe corporate formalities: no board meetings held, no separate corporate records, no annual filings, personal and corporate accounts commingled, corporate funds used for personal expenses; (3) Fraud or injustice: the corporate form is deliberately used to defraud creditors or perpetuate injustice (fraudulent transfers, undercapitalization to avoid creditor claims). Generally, shareholders must have BOTH disregarded corporate formalities AND used the corporation to perpetuate injustice for veil-piercing to succeed. Note: the shareholders' personal guarantees bind them to specific obligations regardless of veil-piercing; veil-piercing would expose them to ALL corporate debts.
explanations.d: Majority control alone does not pierce the veil. Dominant shareholders regularly exercise control without losing limited liability protection — this is normal and expected. The veil-piercing analysis requires something beyond normal shareholder control.

questions.keyword: Business structures — sole proprietorship, general/limited partnership, LLC, C corporation, S corporation: formation, liability protection, continuity, taxation, management; rights and duties of owners
questions.text: Two entrepreneurs are comparing entity structures for a new technology startup. They anticipate significant early losses ($500,000 over 3 years), plan to bring in 5 venture capital investors (3 are foreign nationals, 2 are US-based LLCs), and expect to sell the company in 5-7 years for a significant gain. Analyze which entity structure BEST serves their needs and why.

answers.text: S corporation — pass-through taxation allows founders to deduct early losses against other income; limited liability protects all owners
Sole proprietorship — the founders should not share ownership with outside investors to maintain simplicity and avoid double taxation
General partnership — the simplest structure; all parties are partners; losses flow through to all partners including foreign nationals

C corporation — while early losses don't immediately flow through, C corporations: accommodate foreign shareholders and LLC investors (no S corp restrictions); allow multiple classes of stock (required for VC preferred stock); may qualify for §1202 QSBS exclusion (up to $10M gain excluded at exit); early losses accumulate as NOL carryforwards

explanations.a: S corporations have critical disqualifying limitations for this scenario: (1) Foreign national shareholders are NOT PERMITTED — S corporations can only have US citizens and resident aliens as shareholders. Three of the five VC investors are foreign nationals → they cannot be S shareholders; (2) LLCs cannot be S corporation shareholders (partnerships and corporations generally cannot be S shareholders) → the two US-based LLC investors are also disqualified; (3) One class of stock restriction — S corporations cannot have preferred stock with different economic rights, which VC investors invariably require. S corporation is ELIMINATED by these restrictions.
explanations.b: A sole proprietorship cannot have multiple owners — by definition, it is one-person. It cannot accommodate the founders or VC investors.
explanations.c: General partnership provides no limited liability protection — all partners (including VC investors) have unlimited personal liability. VC funds generally cannot invest in general partnerships (UBTI concerns for their tax-exempt LP investors).
explanations.d: C corporation analysis: (1) Shareholder flexibility: C corporations can have UNLIMITED shareholders of ANY type — foreign nationals, LLCs, corporations, trusts — no restrictions; (2) Multiple classes of stock: C corporations can issue preferred stock with liquidation preferences, participating features, anti-dilution rights — essential for VC investment; (3) §1202 QSBS (Qualified Small Business Stock): founders and early investors in a C corporation may exclude up to $10 million (or 10× basis) of gain from income at exit, if stock is held >5 years and qualifies as QSBS — potentially ELIMINATING capital gains tax on the exit; (4) Early losses: the $500,000 of losses cannot be deducted by shareholders directly (no pass-through), but the corporation accumulates NOL carryforwards; (5) Exit: C corporation stock acquisition or asset sale is straightforward; QSBS provides powerful tax incentive. The QSBS exclusion combined with VC compatibility makes C corporation the optimal structure despite the lack of current loss pass-through.
